questions.q: What is the actual quantity PPO optimizes in the RLHF stage, beyond just the reward model's score?
options: The reward model's score alone, with no other term
The negative of the reward model's score
The KL divergence alone, with the reward model ignored
The reward model's score minus a beta-weighted KL divergence between the current policy and the frozen reference (SFT) model
questions.explain: The total reward is r_RM(x,y) minus beta times the KL divergence between the current policy and the frozen reference model, not the reward model score in isolation.

questions.q: Why is the KL divergence approximated per-token during generation rather than computed exactly?
options: Per-token approximation is more accurate than any exact computation
Reference models cannot produce log-probabilities
Computing the full KL divergence over all possible generated sequences is intractable, so a per-token log-probability difference is used as a cheap Monte Carlo estimate
The reward model requires the KL to be computed per-token by definition
questions.explain: Summing log-probability differences between policy and reference model at each generated token gives a tractable, per-sample estimate that's exact only in expectation.

questions.q: What problem from Chapter 6 does the KL penalty directly help defend against?
options: Reward model overoptimization — the policy exploiting reward model blind spots by drifting toward text the reward model over-scores
Running out of preference data during training
Slow GPU utilization during training
Vanishing gradients in the value head
questions.explain: The KL penalty puts a cost on drifting from the reference model that is independent of the reward model's judgment, providing a check on overoptimization that doesn't rely on the reward model being correct.

questions.q: What problem does a fixed, untuned beta create, and how does adaptive KL control address it?
options: Beta has no effect on training dynamics at all

Too small a beta lets the policy drift too far before the penalty bites, and too large a beta barely lets it move from the SFT model; adaptive control adjusts beta during training to keep KL near a target value
A fixed beta always works perfectly, so adaptive control is unnecessary
Adaptive control eliminates the need for a reference model entirely
questions.explain: A static beta is hard to tune correctly in advance; adaptive KL control strengthens or relaxes beta based on observed KL drift, keeping it near a chosen target throughout training.

questions.q: In the per-token KL approximation code, what two quantities are being subtracted?
options: Two separate reward model scores from an ensemble
The current policy's log-probability of the generated token and the frozen reference model's log-probability of that same token
The learning rate and the clipping range
The reward model's score and the value function's estimate
questions.explain: approx_kl_penalty computes policy_logprobs minus ref_logprobs — the difference in how likely the current policy versus the frozen reference model finds the same generated token.
